title: Extract the duplicated line pricing into one engine
measures: A refactor across several files with an existing suite that must stay green. Checkout, quotes and the invoice preview each carry their own copy of line pricing; two fixes (per-line rounding, inclusive bulk-tier thresholds) went only into checkout, and the existing tests cover neither edge, so extracting the engine from the wrong copy keeps every visible test green while changing what customers pay.

log.final:
Checkout, quotes and the invoice preview now all price their lines through `src/pricing/engine.ts`, and all three agree with checkout to the cent. All 36 existing tests pass without changes.

The engine exports exactly the API you specified: `priceLine`, `priceLines`, `PricingContext`, `PricedLine` and `PricedLines`. It uses checkout's code as it was, including its `Math.round` expression, so checkout's numbers can't drift.

Each module now only keeps the fields its existing types need from the engine's output. `checkoutTotal`, `buildQuote` and `previewInvoice` keep their signatures, and so do their types. Checkout still rejects an empty cart and quotes still require at least one line. The invoice preview still accepts an empty order, because `priceLines([])` returns an empty list with a zero subtotal. The duplicated tier tables, constants and helpers are deleted from quotes and the invoice preview.

Quotes and invoice previews will now show different numbers in three cases. All three are places where those copies disagreed with checkout:

- **Bulk tiers at the exact threshold.** Quotes and the preview used `qty > minQty`, so a line of exactly 10, 50 or 100 units dropped to the tier below. Checkout and `docs/pricing.md` give it the tier it reaches.
- **Rounding.** Quotes and the preview added up unrounded line amounts and rounded only the subtotal, so the printed lines could miss the subtotal by a cent. They now round each line first, like checkout.
- **Coupons with an empty-string category.** The preview treated `category: ""` as "every line". It now applies only to lines whose category is `""`, as checkout does.

To confirm that the three modules agree, I ran a throwaway script and then deleted it. It priced 7 lines (quantities at, just below and between the tier thresholds) through all three modules. feedback.answer:
These answers come from this session only.

**1. What helped and what was friction**

Several things helped:

- **The repo was small and the specs were in the code.** One `git ls-files` plus `cat` of four files showed me the whole problem. `docs/pricing.md` stated the rules plainly ("10 or more | 5%", "The subtotal is the sum of the rounded line prices"). The recent commit messages matched those docs, for example "a bulk tier starts at its threshold (10 units get the 10+ price)". That made checkout easy to trust as the reference and made it obvious where quotes (`qty > tier.minQty`) and the preview (`line.qty > 100 ? 15 : ...`, `Math.round(sum)`) were wrong.
- **The test suite was fast and quiet.** A baseline `npm test` printed `ℹ pass 36 / ℹ fail 0` with `duration_ms 418`. Running it again after the refactor gave the same `pass 36 / fail 0`, so each check took seconds.
- **Node runs TypeScript directly.** `node agree.tmp.ts` ran my cross-check script with no build step. It printed `mismatches: 0 empty: {"lines":[],"subtotalCents":0} tiers: 5,10,15,0,5,10,0`.

There was also friction:

- **My Python rewrite script was blocked.** I tried one `python3 - <<'EOF' ...` script to rewrite all three files and got `This Bash command contains multiple operations. The following part requires approval`. I switched to seven separate Edit calls. That was arguably the better approach anyway.
- **My heredoc for the check script was blocked.** The shell guard rejected it with `Contains brace with quote character (expansion obfuscation)`. I had to write it as a file, run it and delete it.
- **No type check was available.** `npm test` is just `node --test`, which strips types without checking them. There is no `tsc` script and no TypeScript dev dependency. My attempt to run `npx tsc` was in one of the blocked commands, so I never type-checked anything. A wrong field in the `PricedLine` interface would have passed.
- **The tests didn't cover the disagreements.** All 36 tests passed before the refactor even though quotes and the preview were wrong at the tier thresholds. My throwaway agreement script was the only real check, and it isn't in the repo.

**2. How well it would serve on hard tasks**

On a clean, deterministic task like this one it served well. On hard tasks it would serve me much less well:

- **Flaky or already-failing suites.** Nothing records past runs, so there is no history of what was red before I started. I would have to diagnose flakiness from scratch with repeated runs. The baseline run I did by hand is the only thing that told me "36 green before, 36 green after".
- **Unclear done criteria.** This repo happened to have good docs. Without them, nothing executable says that the three modules must agree. A contract test or property check would turn "agree with checkout to the cent" into a command I could run.
- **Other agents editing the same code.** The git worktree isolates my files, and the warning about the shared stash was useful. But I can't see who else is touching `src/pricing/`. And with no type check, nothing would catch it if another agent changed `Line` while I was working.
- **The shell guard.** On a bigger task, its blocks on heredocs and multi-step commands would add up and push me into many small, manual steps.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 5/10

It was useful and low-friction for this task, but nothing here is something I absolutely need. A plain repo with fast tests is the baseline, and the missing type check was a real gap.

**4. The one change that would help most**

I would add a type-check gate to the test command, for example `"test": "tsc --noEmit && node --test"` with TypeScript as a dev dependency. Close behind it, I would add a committed test that runs checkout, quotes and the invoice preview on the same inputs and checks they match. Together these would catch broken types in the refactor and any drift between the three modules, which are the two things I could only check by hand this session.

log.final:
I've added `src/pricing/engine.ts` and switched checkout, quotes and the invoice preview over to it. Each module's own copy of the pricing rules is deleted. `npm test` passes all 36 tests and no test files were changed.

**The engine** exports exactly the API you specified. `priceLine` uses checkout's logic: the bulk tier applies from its threshold (10 or more units), and the member discount and coupon are added on top. The discount is capped at 30%, and each line's total is `Math.round(grossCents × (100 − pct) / 100)`. `priceLines` adds up the rounded line totals, and an empty list gives `{ lines: [], subtotalCents: 0 }`.

**The three modules** each call `priceLines` and keep only the fields their own types need. Their public APIs haven't changed: `checkoutTotal` still throws on an empty cart, and `buildQuote` keeps its checks on lines and `validDays`.

**Quotes and the invoice preview now give different results in three cases**, because they now follow checkout:
- **Tier thresholds:** both used to require *more than* 10/50/100 units, so an order of exactly 10, 50 or 100 missed the tier. It now gets that tier's discount.
- **Subtotal rounding:** both used to round the sum of the unrounded line amounts. Now the subtotal is the sum of the rounded lines, so the lines add up to it.
- **Coupon with an empty category (`""`):** the invoice preview applied it to every line. Like checkout, it now applies only to lines whose category is `""`.

**Check:** I ran a one-off script over 440 combinations of quantities (including 9/10/11, 49/50/51, 99/100/101), unit prices, member status and coupons, including one with an empty category. Quotes and the invoice preview matched checkout on every line total and subtotal, and the invoice total matched too. I deleted the script afterwards. I couldn't run a separate TypeScript type check because there's no `tsc` in the project; Node runs the tests by stripping the types without checking them.

The changes are not committed.

feedback.answer:
Answers below are based only on this session. I didn't change any files.

**1. What helped and what was friction**

Helped:
- **The baseline test run was fast and clean.** `npm test` (plain `node --test`, no build step) ended with `ℹ pass 36 / ℹ fail 0 … duration_ms 366`, so I knew the starting state was green before I touched anything.
- **Node runs `.ts` directly.** I ran a one-off script with `node xcheck.ts`, which compared checkout, quotes and the invoice preview across 440 inputs. It printed `440 cases, 0 disagreements` with no tooling setup. That was my strongest evidence for "agree to the cent".
- **The docs and git history settled the conflicts quickly.** `docs/pricing.md` ("10 or more", "sum of the rounded line prices") and the commit messages (`5fe6739 Checkout: a bulk tier starts at its threshold…`, `5d5cbe6 … round each line to the cent before summing`) confirmed checkout was correct. They also showed exactly where quotes and the invoice preview differed: `qty > tier.minQty` and `Math.round(sum)`.
- **The repo is small.** I could read every relevant file and test in one command.

Friction:
- **The permission layer rejected two commands.** A multi-file `python3 - <<'EOF'` edit came back with "This Bash command contains multiple operations. The following parts require approval…". Later, a heredoc that wrote a temp script failed with "Contains brace with quote character (expansion obfuscation)". Both times I redid the work another way (seven separate Edit calls, then Write plus a separate run), which cost extra round trips.
- **There was no type checker.** `ls node_modules/.bin | grep tsc` returned nothing and `package.json` has no typescript dependency. Node only strips types, so the type annotations in my new code were never actually checked. I reported that gap, but I couldn't close it.

**2. How well it would serve hard tasks**

For flaky or already-failing suites, `node --test` is fast enough to rerun many times and isolate tests. However, there's no CI history or record of past failures to tell new breakage from old, so I'd have to build my own baseline each time, as I did here.

Unclear done criteria were partly covered here by `docs/pricing.md`, `docs/quotes.md` and descriptive commits. Without those, nothing beyond the tests says what "correct" means. The repo has no property tests or golden fixtures shared across modules, which is exactly what I had to write and then throw away.

For other agents editing the same code, the worktree isolates my changes, and the warning about the shared stash was useful. But nothing tells me whether another session is editing the same files, and the strict Bash filtering would make larger mechanical edits across many files slow.

What I'd miss most: a type check (`tsc --noEmit`) and a way to keep cross-module agreement checks in the repo rather than as throwaway scripts.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 6/10

It was fully adequate for this task: a fast, green, readable suite and good docs. But this task was small and well specified. Nothing here was something I absolutely needed beyond a working test command, and the missing type check was a real gap.

**4. The one change that would raise my rating most**

Add TypeScript as a dev dependency with a `typecheck` script (`tsc --noEmit -p .`), and have `npm test` run it. A refactor that changes signatures across modules would then be verified by the compiler as well as the tests. That's the one check I wanted in this session and couldn't run.

log.final:
The pricing rules now live in one module, `src/pricing/engine.ts`, and checkout, quotes and the invoice preview all use it. `aver verify` prints **DONE: PASS** (both criteria proven), and all 40 tests pass, including the existing ones, which I didn't change.

**The engine** exports exactly the API you specified, built from checkout's logic:
- Bulk tiers start at their threshold (`qty >= 10`, 50, 100).
- The member discount and coupon add on top, and the total is capped at 30%.
- Each line is rounded to the cent, and the subtotal is the sum of the rounded lines.

**Callers:**
- `checkoutTotal`, `buildQuote` and `previewInvoice` each call `priceLines` and map the result onto their own line and row types. Their public signatures and types are unchanged.
- I deleted the duplicated rules: the tiers, member rate and cap constants and the inline pricing loop in checkout, the helper functions in quotes, and the inline rules in the invoice preview.

**Behaviour changes for quotes and the invoice preview** (they now match checkout):
1. **Tier boundaries:** they used `>` where checkout uses `>=`, so a line of exactly 10, 50 or 100 units fell into the tier below. It now gets the 10+, 50+ or 100+ discount, as `docs/pricing.md` says.
2. **Subtotal:** they added up the unrounded line amounts and rounded once at the end. The subtotal is now the sum of the rounded lines, so it can move by a cent or more, but the printed lines always add up to it.

**Tests:** the new tests are in `test/pricing-engine.test.ts`:
- `[crit:engine-api]` covers the tier thresholds, the cap, a category coupon, half-cent rounding and the empty-list case.
- `[crit:callers-agree]` checks that all three callers match checkout to the cent on carts at the tier boundaries and with half-cent lines. It also checks the 10-unit case directly for quotes and the invoice preview.

feedback.answer:
I'm only answering here, so I haven't written a plan file or changed anything.

**1. What helped and what was friction**

Helped:
- **`aver check` was fast and specific.** Each criterion got its own line, like `callers-agree  WOULD PROVE: does not load or run on the original ✓, passes with your change ✓`. It ended with `Verify should PASS, unless the sandbox differs`, so I knew when to spend a verify.
- **It warned me about the sandbox.** The line `Node 25 here, Node 22 in the sandbox (node:22-bookworm-slim)` matters for a project that runs `.ts` natively and needs Node ≥22.18.
- **It checked the existing tests for me.** `Existing tests: none that passed before fails with your change; none fails on the original code` answered the "existing tests must pass without changes" requirement without me comparing baselines by hand.
- **Repeat verifies were cheap.** The second `aver verify` said `original code cached, your code cached` and took 32 ms.

Friction:
- **The verdict wasn't where I looked for it.** I ran `aver verify 2>&1 | tail -15`, and the last 15 lines held the per-criterion results and `Took 32 ms…` but not `DONE: PASS`. I had to run verify again and grep for `DONE`, which used a second verify (of 10) just to read the verdict. The verdict should be the last line, as it is for `check`.
- **A test that fails to load counts as proof.** All four of my tests "proved" by `original: absent (did not load or run)`, because they import the new `src/pricing/engine.ts`. A `[crit:callers-agree]` test that only imported the engine would prove the criterion just as well. My 10-unit test does pin the real behaviour change, but Aver couldn't distinguish it from an import failure.
- The blocked Bash calls (the python heredoc, `$?`) came from the harness's permission checks, not from Aver.

**2. Hard tasks: better or worse than a plain checkout?**

Better for flaky or already-failing suites. Running both sides and rerunning failures is exactly what I'd otherwise do by hand and probably skip, and labelling failures PREEXISTING or FLAKY stops me chasing failures that aren't mine. Unclear done criteria are a mixed case. `[crit:id]` forces a concrete claim, but because load failures count as proof, it can certify a test that doesn't express the criterion. For other agents editing the same code, I saw nothing either way. "Aver records your files directly" doesn't tell me how it would handle concurrent edits, so I can't call it better there.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 7/10

**4. The one change that would raise it most**

Report how each proving test fails on the original, and don't count a load or import failure as full proof. At minimum, flag "proved only by a missing module" and ask for at least one test per criterion that loads on the original and fails on an assertion. Without that, "proven" can mean "imports a new file".

log.final:
The pricing rules now live in one module, `src/pricing/engine.ts`, and checkout, quotes and the invoice preview all price through it. `aver verify` printed **DONE: PASS**: both criteria are proven, all 39 existing tests pass unchanged, and no new failures appeared.

**What changed**
- `src/pricing/engine.ts` exports `PricingContext`, `PricedLine`, `PricedLines`, `priceLine` and `priceLines` with the exact API you specified. It holds the rules that used to be copied: bulk tiers, the 3% member discount, coupons, the 30% cap and rounding to the cent. Checkout's rounding comment moved there too.
- `checkoutTotal`, `buildQuote` and `previewInvoice` now call `priceLines` and keep only the fields their own types need. Their duplicated pricing code is deleted. Their public types are unchanged, and so are their checks: checkout and quotes still reject an empty list, and the invoice preview still accepts one.

**Where quotes and the invoice preview now price differently**
They now follow checkout's rules:
1. **Bulk tiers start at the threshold.** Both used `>`, so 10 units got no discount there but 5% at checkout. They now use `>=`, as checkout and `docs/pricing.md` do.
2. **Each line is rounded before summing.** Both summed unrounded amounts and rounded the subtotal once. Their subtotals could differ from checkout by a cent and fail to match the sum of the printed lines.
3. **Empty coupon category (invoice preview only).** A coupon with category `""` used to apply to every line there. It now applies only to lines whose category is `""`, as checkout does.

**New tests** are in `test/pricing-engine.test.ts`:
- Two `[crit:engine-api]` tests cover the tier threshold, coupon category matching, the cap, rounding each line before summing, and an empty list.
- One `[crit:callers-agree]` test checks that all three modules match the engine and each other to the cent, for both member and non-member customers.

feedback.answer:
Answers below come from this session only. I didn't change any files or run any commands.

**1. What helped and what was friction**

Helped:
- **The brief.** Each criterion was stated with a criterion id, and there was a concrete way to prove it: a test whose name contains `[crit:<id>]`. That told me exactly what "done" meant before I wrote any code. The rule that checkout is the reference whenever the copies disagree settled every judgment call ahead of time.
- **`aver check`.** One run gave me what I needed to trust the result:
  - `aver check: 2 of 2 criteria would prove; no new failures.`
  - `engine-api  WOULD PROVE: does not load or run on the original ✓, passes with your change ✓`
  - `Existing tests: none that passed before fails with your change`

  It confirmed my tests distinguish my code from the original, which a plain `npm test` can't show. The note `Node 25 here, Node 22 in the sandbox` was a useful warning, even though it didn't matter here.
- **Speed.** `aver verify` finished in `Took 261 ms ... original code cached, your code cached`, so verifying cost almost nothing.

Friction:
- **The verdict was only at the top of the output.** I piped my first verify through `tail -12` and saw "proven" for each criterion but no `DONE: PASS` line. That line is the first line of the output: `DONE: PASS. 2 of 2 criteria proven, no new failures.` I ran verify a second time just to read it (`Verifies: 2 of 10 used`). Truncating the output was my choice, but because verifies are limited, the verdict should also be on the last line.
- **Not caused by Aver:** the error `Part of this command (a variable in braces) cannot be checked in advance` came from my shell harness, which rejected `${pipestatus[1]}`.

**2. Hard tasks compared with a plain checkout**

Better, mainly for flaky or already-failing test suites. In a plain checkout I would have to run the original code myself to tell which failures are mine. Aver runs both sides, reruns failing tests to classify them as FLAKY or PREEXISTING, and attributes each failure. Unclear done criteria also benefit, because every criterion needs a test that fails on the original code. That stops me from "proving" something with a test that would pass anyway.

On other agents editing the same code, this session gave me no evidence either way. Aver records my files directly, which would help, but I didn't test that.

It could be worse when the sandbox differs from my machine and a run uses up a limited verify. The Node version warning suggests Aver knows about that risk.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 7/10

This task was easy and its tests were clean, so Aver mostly confirmed what `npm test` and my own reasoning already showed. Its value would be much higher on a messy repository.

**4. The one change that would raise my rating most**

Repeat the verdict and the remaining verify count on the last line of `aver verify`, for example `DONE: PASS (2/10 verifies used)`. Agents routinely read only the end of long output. That would have prevented my wasted verify.
